lab_title: Exploring VSEPR Theory and Molecular Geometry
top_level_objectives: Apply VSEPR theory to predict the 3D arrangements of electron domains around a central atom.
Distinguish between electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry.
Explain how lone pairs influence bond angles and cause deviations from idealized geometries.
Predict the molecular shapes of compounds with expanded octets including trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral derivatives.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the fundamental force driving VSEPR theory by letting students feel and see electron domains repelling one another to maximize their separation.
key_visuals: A central atomic nucleus floating in AR space.
Interactive electron domain lobes represented as translucent, glowing clouds.
Real-time repulsive force vectors shown as dynamic arrows indicating push direction and strength.
student_actions: Manually grab and try to push two electron domains close together, feeling the virtual resistance.
Add up to six electron domains to the central atom and watch them automatically self-organize into symmetric arrangements.
Toggle a force vector overlay to visualize how repulsion drops to a minimum when domains are furthest apart.

scenes.brief_purpose: Examine the five basic spatial arrangements that minimize repulsion for two, three, four, five, and six electron domains.
key_visuals: Five distinct 3D models floating in a semi-circle: linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral.
Color-coded domains indicating axial vs. equatorial positions where relevant.
Angle overlays displaying the exact geometric angles (e.g., 180, 120, 109.5, 90 degrees).
student_actions: Walk around and scale each of the five basic structures to study them from multiple perspectives.
Match the correct geometric name label to each of the floating 3D models.
Rotate the trigonal bipyramidal model to identify the difference between the 90-degree axial and 120-degree equatorial positions.

scenes.scene_name: Lone Pairs vs. Bonding Pairs in Tetrahedral Systems
scenes.brief_purpose: Illustrate how replacing bonding pairs with non-bonding lone pairs transforms the apparent molecular shape while keeping the electron-domain geometry tetrahedral.
key_visuals: Three parallel molecular templates representing Methane (CH4), Ammonia (NH3), and Water (H2O).
Visible differences in representation: bonding pairs shown as solid sticks to terminal atoms, and lone pairs shown as large, bulbous, pulsating charge clouds.
Dynamic text labels transitioning between Electron Geometry and Molecular Geometry names.
student_actions: Tap a bonding domain on a tetrahedral methane molecule to convert it into a lone pair, witnessing the transition to the trigonal pyramidal ammonia geometry.
Convert another bonding domain to a lone pair to witness the transition to the bent water geometry.
Compare the final visual envelopes of the three molecules to understand why lone pairs are invisible to molecular shape detection but dictate spatial positioning.

scenes.scene_name: Lone Pair Repulsion and Bond Angle Compression
scenes.brief_purpose: Explain why lone pairs occupy more space than bonding pairs, leading to measurable deviations from ideal bond angles.
key_visuals: An interactive water molecule side-by-side with a methane molecule.
A highlighted radial volume dial showing the physical space occupied by a bonding electron pair versus a lone pair.
Interactive bond angle arcs that update dynamically.
student_actions: Adjust a 'Repulsion Magnitude' slider for the lone pairs to see how their expansion forces the adjacent O-H bonds closer together.
Measure the resulting compressed bond angle of water (104.5 degrees) and compare it directly to methane's ideal tetrahedral angle (109.5 degrees).
Place a virtual protractor over ammonia (NH3) to confirm its intermediate bond angle of 107 degrees.

scenes.scene_name: Expanded Octets: Seesaw, T-Shape, and Square Planar
scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate the critical importance of equatorial versus axial placement of lone pairs in expanded valence shells.
key_visuals: A trigonal bipyramidal template (PF5) and an octahedral template (SF6).
An 'Energy Level' meter that fills or empties based on the stability of lone pair placements.
Highlight indicators showing the 90-degree interactions that cause high-energy repulsion.
student_actions: Drag a lone pair onto an axial position of a trigonal bipyramidal molecule and observe the high-repulsion warning indicator.
Relocate the lone pair to an equatorial position to find the lower-energy state, forming a stable Seesaw molecular geometry.
Assemble Sulfur Tetrafluoride (SF4), Chlorine Trifluoride (ClF3), and Xenon Tetrafluoride (XeF4) by placing the correct number of lone pairs in their optimal geometric positions.

scenes.brief_purpose: Synthesize knowledge of VSEPR theory by analyzing uncharacterized compounds, determining their structures, and verifying with real physical data.
key_visuals: A virtual laboratory workbench displaying a set of chemical formulas (e.g., SF6, XeF4, NH3).
An interactive 'VSEPR Workbench' containing customizable central atoms, bond sticks, and lone pair widgets.
A 'Spectrum Analyzer' portal that reveals actual experimentally determined molecular shapes upon correct assembly.
student_actions: Select a chemical formula card and calculate its total valence electron count and electron domains.
Construct the correct 3D molecular geometry on the workbench by dragging bonding pairs and lone pairs into position.
Submit the constructed model to trigger the experimental comparison overlay, checking if their VSEPR prediction matches the real-world physical structure.
